title: Reservoir-based connection pool + probabilistic load-shedding for cross-region Redis & Kafka resilience
creator: Liam Chen
description: Background: We frequently see tail-latency and connection-exhaustion issues during regional spikes or downstream slowdowns (Redis/Kafka). Current connection pools are simple size-limited stacks that allow head-of-line blocking: when downstream slows, in-flight requests pile up and cause cascading resource exhaustion across the serving runtime. This ticket implements a reservoir-based pool with probabilistic shedding + circuit annealing and cross-region reroute policies to keep user-visible SLOs intact while preserving degraded but functional behavior.
goals: Introduce a reservoir-style connection allocator that exposes a deterministic token count per instance and per-region so we avoid unbounded connection growth
Implement probabilistic load-shedding for requests that would otherwise block beyond a short grace window
Add a circuit 'annealing' mechanism that slowly reopens a downstream when it appears healthy and avoids flapping
Enable region-aware failover routing for critical read paths with configurable priority tiers
Ship observability (metrics, dashboards, alerts) and a runbook for operators
non_goals: Full rewrite of Redis/Kafka client libraries — we will wrap existing clients
Application-level schema changes or index-level DB optimizations
Replacing global routing or deployment topology
design_summary: We will implement a token-based reservoir that is sized from per-host concurrency budget and downstream capability profiles. Tokens represent parallel requests that may hold a connection/stream. When tokens are exhausted we do not block indefinitely: short optimistic wait (50ms) then apply a probabilistic drop with a drop probability that ramps with queue depth and recent error-rate signals. Circuit states: CLOSED, OPEN, and ANNEALING. OPEN is entered when error-rate or 95th latency breaches configurable thresholds for a window. ANNEALING is a controlled slow re-open phase where a small percentage of requests are allowed through and observed; success moves to CLOSED, failures back to OPEN. Cross-region policy: when local reservoir is unavailable, the router consults a priority list: same-region replicas -> sibling-region warm pool -> global fallback model (if configured). Failures are logged and emit SLO impact events for postmortem.
implementation_notes: Reservoir sizing: base_tokens = floor(cpu_cores * concurrency_per_core * safety_factor) per instance
Short-wait window: 50ms (configurable via feature flag) to absorb microbursts
Probabilistic shedding function: p_drop = min(1, alpha * (queue_len / base_tokens) + beta * recent_error_rate)
Circuit thresholds: 60s evaluation window, OPEN if error_rate > 3% or p95 latency > configured_target for 3 consecutive windows
Annealing policy: linear ramp from 1% -> 20% allowed over 2 minutes if no errors
Kafka specifics: prefer read-from-local-consumer-group when possible; for partition leader failures, route to replica consumers with backpressure tokens
Redis specifics: prioritize local primaries for writes, but reads can preferentially serve from local replicas; write failures trigger immediate token reclaim
Compatibility: implement as middleware layer in the runtime request dispatcher to avoid per-client changes
acceptance_criteria: Unit and integration tests covering reservoir token lifecycle, probabilistic drop curve, and circuit transitions
Staging canary demonstrates >=30% reduction in tail latency (p99) for Redis-bound requests under synthetic downstream delay injection
Alerting and dashboard: SLO burn rate, reservoir token utilization, shed-rate, circuit state per-region are visible in Console
Runbook updated and validated by on-call in a deliberate 'game day' exercise
Gradual rollout plan (10% -> 50% -> 100%) with automatic rollback on high-error budget burn
tasks: Prototype reservoir allocator in runtime dispatcher (ENG)
Add probabilistic shedding module and config knobs (ENG)
Instrument metrics and wire to Console dashboards (Observability)
Create annealing controller and unit tests (ENG)
Integration tests against Redis & Kafka test harness with fault injection (QA)
Canary rollout and monitoring review with PM/Design for UX messaging
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Overly aggressive shedding may drop legitimate traffic -> Mitigation: conservative default curve, feature flag, and fast rollback
Risk: Complex interactions with existing autoscalers -> Mitigation: coordinate with autoscaling team and emit a compatibility metric for autoscaler adjustments
Risk: Mis-sized reservoirs on heterogeneous machines -> Mitigation: add telemetry to compute per-host recommended sizing and a rollout step to tune constants
Risk: Circuit flapping during flakey network -> Mitigation: annealing stage and hysteresis on thresholds
rollout_plan: Phase 1: feature-flagged prototype running in staging with synthetic failures (2 weeks). Phase 2: internal canary (10% of traffic) in non-critical region, 72h observation. Phase 3: expand to 50% with monitoring alarms enabled. Phase 4: global deploy and follow-up tuning. Automatic rollback triggers: >2x SLO burn-rate in 1h or >0.5% absolute error-rate increase over baseline in 30m.
observability: Metrics: reservoir_tokens_total, reservoir_tokens_in_use, shed_rate, shed_rate_by_endpoint, circuit_state{region,downstream}, anneal_pass_rate
Traces: annotate span when request was shed or routed cross-region
Dashboards: per-region SLO burn, token-utilization heatmap, shed_rate trend
Alerts: shed_rate > 5% for 15m on production, circuit_open_count > 0 for 5m on critical downstreams

notes: This approach is intentionally pragmatic: middleware-level reservoir + shedding avoids invasive client changes while giving fine-grained control over degradation behavior. We'll iterate on the drop curve after canary telemetry.
